The Jewish State Solution Proposal

15 Sep 2026 by Sufian M′Barki

When it comes to the situation in the Middle East, countless possibilities have already been entertained and even attempted unsuccessfully. I believe that this prompts a much more ethically and logically rigorous proposal that carries the lowest overall risk - significantly less room for failure ascertained by adequate threat management, international cooperation and logistical relief, medical and psychotherapeutic countermeasures, verified historical precedent, and the standing of surrounding nation-states on the matter.

To understand the feasibility and soundness of this proposal, as well as the exhaustive justification in favor of said proposal, we must first take a look at Israel's history.

The British Mandate of Palestine

Following the events of World War I, Great Britain conquered a piece of the former Ottoman Empire, which it mandated for a couple of decades.

A mandate is a temporary legislative structure which exists to decide the future of the territories it currently governs. Despite this, the British Mandate of Palestine did not function as a benign entity seeking to make an ethical decision for the fate of the land. Instead, Mandate Palestine functioned as yet another colonial outpost for Great Britain, making life especially difficult for Jews attempting to escape from the global rise of antisemitism, as well as the Shoah during World War II. This is to say that the British Mandate was proactively getting in the way of Jews from the Diaspora re-entering their ancestral homeland of Israel, despite the presence of Arab, Ottoman Turkic, and Muslim colonizers in general.

While Israel was under foreign colonial rule, the Muslim population living there alleged that they wanted their own state, and did not want to co-exist with the Jewish population. Meanwhile, Jews had the legitimate claim to their indigenous homeland. Despite this, in a bizarre turn of events, the Western Great Powers made the decision to deploy a Two-State Solution instead.

Between 1921 and 1922, the British Mandate governorate attempted the First Two-State Solution. They agreed to separate the territory east of the Jordan River and establish the Emirate of Transjordan under Emir Abdullah I. Soon after, Abdullah officially established the local government on April 11, 1921.

This Emirate represented about 77% of the territories previously controlled by the British Mandate, and while the remaining 23% were supposedly reserved for the re-establishment of the Jewish State, the Mandate instead declared that the future of those particular territories was undecided.

The local Muslim population was evidently not satisfied with receiving 77% (a massive chunk) of the British Mandate[1]. They insisted on gaining more territories because of their refusal to co-exist with Jews, as well as their perceived claim to the Land of Zion. It is for this reason that when Arabs who lived in Mandate Palestine were also referred to as "Palestinians" during that period, they openly rejected the label because "Palestinian" meant "Israeli" or "a person of the Jewish homeland."

The explanation is simple. The term "Palestine" (or "Syria-Palæstina") was invented by the Roman Empire who had colonized Israel and Judah at the time of its existence. After the Jewish Bar Kokhba Revolt in 132-136 CE, which attempted to liberate the Jewish homeland from the Romans, Emperor Hadrian renamed the entire region to "Syria-Palæstina".

This replaced an ethnically Jewish name (Judæa, "Land of the Jews/Judah") with a geographic term linked to the Philistines (Palæstina), Israel's ancient coastal enemies, who no longer existed as a distinct polity. My historical research into the indigenous name of Azzah provides extra details on the matter, which could not be more relevant:

Philistines were an Ancient Greek tribe, and their colonial settlement was situated around the city of Azzah in the form of a pentapolis. As it has been previously established, they were far from a benign, peaceful tribe. In fact, Philistia was Ancient Israel and Judah's adversary, and they waged aggressive conflict against Jews on numerous occasions.

(...)

Once David defeated Goliath in battle, the Israelites managed to retrieve the small piece of land previously occupied by Philistines, defeating their ancient adversary.

(...)

The city of Azzah is over 5000 years old, and it belonged to the Ancient Canaanites (including Israelites). It began in the Early Bronze Age as an indigenous Canaanite cultural and agricultural hub with major archaeological sites like Tell es-Sakan. The term "Philistine" (and thus the Roman term "Palestine") originates from the Hebrew "פלשת" - or, the Semitic root "פ-ל-ש," which means invader.

Not only does "Palestine" refer to the Jewish homeland of Israel, but the term quite literally comes from the Semitic root for an invader.

Clearly, Muslim Arabs agreed with the meaning for a long time, and their rejection of the term "Palestinian" was a rejection of being called Jewish, or of being described as belonging to the Jewish homeland.

Despite this self-evident truth, another solution was proposed - a unified landmass, neither Jewish nor Muslim. Both populations rejected the idea, and Jews had a good reason to do so - retrieving their homeland for their own self-determination and independence was non-negotiable, considering their millennia-long history of being persecuted, hunted, and massacred. Muslim Arabs only rejected it because of their continued refusal to co-exist with Jews.

When the problem was instead transferred to the United Nations, their final proposal was yet another two-state solution. This was the Second Two-State Solution (the UN Partition of 1947), which would have resulted in one Jewish state and two Islamic states originating from the British Mandate.

Despite this deeply unfair offer, Jews accepted it unanimously. However, Muslims were still dissatisfied, and they rejected the UN Partition as well.

Due to the growing unrest in the Land of Zion, and the existential necessity for security after the most brutal genocide committed against Jews in history, the Jewish underground and populace mounted unified resistance against British administrative blockades. On May 14, 1948, as the Mandate expired, the Jewish State formally declared its independence, receiving immediate recognition from global powers.

Immediately following this declaration, surrounding Arab armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq invaded the renascent Jewish state with the explicit intent to annihilate it.

A great number of Arabs left the territory due to their refusal to co-exist with a sovereign Jewish population. Others left because regional Arab leaders encouraged evacuation - promising a swift military sweep to cleanse the land before re-distributing property - while many fled the active combat zones initiated by the Arab invasion.

Israel successfully repelled the multi-front assault, securing its sovereignty in the 1948-1949 War of Independence. Arab discourse came to define this defeat as the "Nakba" (Arabic for "Catastrophe"). The Arab residents who remained within Israel's borders were integrated as citizens with equal legal rights, formally invited by Israel's foundational charter to participate in the construction of the state[2].

The 1967 Khartoum Resolution: The "Three Nos"

Immediately following the defensive victory of the Six-Day War in June 1967 - wherein Israel pre-empted an existential annihilation campaign spearheaded by Egypt, Syria, and Jordan - Israel's national unity government made direct diplomatic overtures. Israel signaled its willingness to return righteously captured territories in exchange for formal peace treaties, defensible borders, and regional recognition.

The Arab League's response at the Khartoum Summit on September 1, 1967, established the infamous doctrine known as the "Three Nos":

  • No peace with Israel.
  • No recognition of Israel.
  • No negotiations with Israel.

Rather than bargaining for statehood or territorial administration, regional Arab leadership chose utter rejection over peaceful coexistence once more.

The 2000 Camp David Summit (Ehud Barak)

In July 2000, Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak convened with US President Bill Clinton and Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasser Arafat at Camp David. Barak presented an unprecedented offer to establish an independent Arab state:

  • Israeli withdrawal from approximately 91% to 92% of Judea-Samaria (rising to over 95% when factoring in sovereign Israeli land swaps).
  • A sovereign capital in Arab neighborhoods of East Jerusalem.
  • Complete administrative control over 100% of Azzah.
  • Custodianship over religious sites on the Temple Mount.
  • An international multi-billion compensation mechanism for refugees.

The Israeli Prime Minister was ready to delegate a massive chunk of Israeli territory directly to Arab leadership in an attempt to establish regional peace.

Unfortunately, Yasser Arafat not only rejected the offer outright without presenting a counter-proposal, but he returned to Ramallah and launched the Second Intifada - a pre-planned, coordinated campaign of suicide bombings, bus bombings, and civilian café massacres executed by Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and Fatah-affiliated militias. President Clinton later placed the failure of the summit explicitly and squarely on Arafat.

The events in July 2000 reveal that Arab leaders have never been interested in any solutions that involve Israel's continued existence, as well as the existence of coordinated terrorist massacres ready to be deployed if their absurdities are not satisfied.

The 2001 Taba Summit & The Clinton Parameters

To definitively test the principle of "Land for Peace" without waiting for an elusive negotiating partner, Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon executed the Unilateral Disengagement from Azzah in August 2005[3].

Israel made immense, painful domestic sacrifices:

The result of this total Israeli withdrawal was catastrophic. Rather than building a functional, independent society, the local population elected Hamas in 2006. In 2007, Hamas launched a bloody civil war, throwing rival Palestinian Authority officials off high-rise buildings, taking total tyrannical control, and transforming Azzah into a fortified terrorist base.
